title: Not Every Clause Deserves to Survive: Teaching a Summarizer What's Safe to Cut
body:
A sentence pulled straight out of a news article and dropped into a summary keeps everything: its subordinate clause, its parenthetical aside, its throat-clearing preamble. Extractive summarization can only keep a sentence whole or throw it away — it has no way to trim.

That's the gap this project sits in. Extractive summarization is robust but verbose. Abstractive summarization is flexible but hard to control and hard to evaluate. And naive compression — just deleting words until a sentence is shorter — tends to leave you with something that reads like it was hit by a car. The goal here is a summarizer that picks the right sentences *and* knows which words inside them it's actually safe to cut.

## Extraction, then compression — not one or the other

The system, called **JECS**, is a neural extractive summarizer with syntactic compression bolted on — and it splits the job into two stages instead of asking one model to do everything at once.

The extractive half ranks sentences. A **BiLSTM sentence encoder** turns each sentence's words into a representation; a **CNN document encoder** turns those sentence representations into a picture of the whole document; a decoder ranks every sentence against that picture and keeps the top candidates. Word to sentence, sentence to document, document back down to a ranking — a straight pipeline.

The compressive half only ever sees sentences that already survived extraction. A contextualized encoder re-reads them, a compression encoder proposes what could be deleted, and a feed-forward binary classifier makes the call: keep, or delete. Running compression *after* extraction — not folded into the same step — turns out to matter: it keeps the two problems modular and the optimization stable, instead of one messy joint objective that's hard to train.

## Not every clause is safe to cut

Deleting words at random is how you end up with a sentence that technically got shorter and stopped making sense. So the compression candidates aren't chosen freely — they're generated by constituency parsing, restricted to categories that are usually safe to lose:

- Appositive noun phrases
- Relative and adverbial clauses
- Adjective phrases inside noun phrases
- Gerundive verb phrases
- Selected prepositional phrases
- Parenthetical expressions

Every deletion the classifier is even allowed to propose comes from this syntactic list. That constraint is the whole point: it's what keeps aggressive trimming from turning into aggressive damage.

## How much to cut is its own problem

Even with the syntax rules in place, compression has a dial, and where you set it matters. Push it lightly and ROUGE scores go up — the summary says more per word. Push it too hard and scores fall again, because the model starts deleting things it shouldn't, and grammaticality erodes along with it. The threshold isn't a detail to tune once and forget; it's the trade-off the whole system is built around — information density against grammaticality, with a real cost on either side of the line.

## Testing it against everything else in the field

JECS was evaluated on three datasets with different compressibility characteristics — CNN, CNN/DailyMail (CNNDM), and New York Times (NYT) — against a wide field of baselines: Lead, LeadDedup, LeadComp, Extraction-only, Refresh, LatSum, BanditSum, and, on CNNDM specifically, NeuSum, LatSum with compression, CBDec, and FARS. Scoring ran on ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L, plus a human grammaticality evaluation on Amazon Mechanical Turk and manual error analysis — because a summary that scores well on ROUGE and reads badly to a person hasn't actually solved the problem.

**CNN**

| Model | ROUGE-1 | ROUGE-2 | ROUGE-L |
|-----------------|---------|---------|---------|
| Lead (Ours) | 29.1 | 11.1 | 25.8 |
| Refresh | 30.3 | 11.6 | 26.9 |
| LatSum | 28.8 | 11.5 | 25.4 |
| BanditSum | 30.7 | 11.6 | 27.4 |
| LeadDedup | 29.7 | 10.9 | 26.2 |
| LeadComp | 30.6 | 10.8 | 27.2 |
| Extraction | 30.3 | 11.0 | 26.5 |
| ExtLSTMDEL | 30.6 | 11.9 | 27.1 |
| **JECS** | **32.7** | **12.2** | **29.0** |

**CNN / DailyMail (CNNDM)**

| Model | ROUGE-1 | ROUGE-2 | ROUGE-L |
|------------------------|---------|---------|---------|
| Lead (Ours) | 40.3 | 17.6 | 36.4 |
| Refresh | 40.0 | 18.1 | 36.6 |
| NeuSum | 41.6 | 19.0 | 38.0 |
| LatSum | 41.0 | 18.8 | 37.4 |
| LatSum w/ Compression | 36.7 | 15.4 | 34.3 |
| BanditSum | 41.5 | 18.7 | 37.6 |
| CBDec | 40.7 | 17.9 | 37.1 |
| FARS | 40.9 | 17.8 | 38.5 |
| LeadDedup | 40.5 | 17.4 | 36.5 |
| LeadComp | 40.8 | 17.4 | 36.8 |
| Extraction | 40.7 | 18.0 | 36.8 |
| **JECS** | **41.7** | **18.5** | **37.9** |

**New York Times (NYT)**

| Model | ROUGE-1 | ROUGE-2 | ROUGE-L |
|------------|---------|---------|---------|
| Lead | 41.8 | 22.6 | 35.0 |
| LeadDedup | 42.0 | 22.8 | 35.0 |
| LeadComp | 42.4 | 22.7 | 35.4 |
| Extraction | 44.3 | 25.5 | 37.1 |
| **JECS** | **45.5** | **25.3** | **38.2** |

Notice LatSum with compression on CNNDM: adding compression to that model actually *hurt* it, dropping ROUGE-1 from 41.0 to 36.7. That's the aggressive-compression failure mode showing up in someone else's numbers, not just in theory.

## What actually convinced people, not just the metric

ROUGE is a proxy. The real test was Amazon Mechanical Turk workers rating grammaticality directly, alongside a manual error count.

| Model | Preference (%) ↑ | Error ↓ | ROUGE-1 ↑ |
|--------------|------------------|---------|-----------|
| Ext LEAD3 | – | 22 | 29.1 |
| ExtDROP | 12% | 161 | 30.2 |
| ExtLSTMDEL | 43% | **24** | 30.6 |
| **JECS** | **45%** | 31 | **32.7** |

JECS won the highest human preference at 45% and the best ROUGE-1 among this group at 32.7, though ExtLSTMDEL still edged it on raw error count. Grammaticality and information density don't move in perfect lockstep — which is exactly why both had to be measured.

## The takeaway

Compression only pays off when it knows what it's allowed to touch. Splitting extraction from compression, and constraining the deletions to syntactic categories instead of raw word-dropping, is what let JECS gain information density without losing the grammatical ground extractive summarization already had. If you're building a summarizer and reaching for compression, start by asking not how much to cut, but what categories of phrase are actually safe to lose.
